Financial planning · The currency of a future bill · Visual planning guide

Foreign-currency cash can match a foreign bill while its CAD value still moves

Use four interactive charts to translate earmarked cash and a fixed foreign bill together, distinguish allocation from funding and compare the remaining exposure to a terminal exchange quote.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Match the currency of a known bill and translate both sides

Interactive planning lab

Share of the fixed foreign bill funded at the bill date95.00%
Cash available less the bill, measured in its own currency-1,000 FCU
Funding position translated into CAD at the bill date-$1,500

Original hypothetical cash-matching illustration for one fixed nominal bill in generic foreign-currency units (FCU). Both quotes are CAD paid per one FCU and are independent assumptions, not observed or forecast exchange rates. The selected share of the starting CAD budget is converted immediately at the starting quote; the remainder stays in CAD. Both cash balances then earn zero until the single bill date. Foreign cash is used directly in the bill’s currency and remaining CAD cash is converted at the terminal quote. CAD values are reporting translations, not an assumed sale and repurchase of the foreign cash. There are no conversion spreads, fees, taxes, deposit interest, price changes in the foreign bill, transfer delays, account failures or other household assets. A funding position is these earmarked resources less this one bill; it is not a full household net-worth statement or a present value. Allocating 100% to foreign cash removes terminal-quote sensitivity of the FCU amount under these assumptions, but does not fix an initially inadequate budget or establish that the account and payment route are suitable.

The central idea

The currency of the goal matters beside the currency used to report account value. Translate both the earmarked resources and the bill before interpreting an exchange-rate gain.

01

Write the bill in the currency that must actually be paid

A fixed foreign-currency bill can become more expensive in Canadian dollars without changing in its own currency. A cash account held in that foreign currency also changes in reported CAD value. Looking at only one side can misstate progress toward the goal.

This example uses a generic foreign-currency unit, or FCU. The bill is 20,000 FCU on one future payment date. Its amount is assumed fixed: there is no additional foreign-price inflation or change in the purchase itself.

The Bank of Canada’s daily-rate page expresses foreign exchange as CAD for one unit of foreign currency and describes its published rates as indicative averages. The quotes here follow that unit convention but are independently chosen assumptions. They are not observed rates, provider quotes or forecasts.

02

Start every currency choice with the same CAD budget

The default budget is CAD 27,000, equal to the bill’s reference cost at the assumed starting quote of 1.35 CAD per FCU. The selected allocation converts half of that budget at the start: CAD 13,500 becomes 10,000 FCU. The other CAD 13,500 remains in CAD cash.

Both cash balances earn zero in the illustration. There is no outside contribution, investment gain or spending before the bill. The alternative paths use the same CAD 27,000 and starting quote, changing only the share converted initially.

This matching of starting resources matters. A comparison that gives one currency choice more capital would mix a funding advantage with an exchange-rate effect.

03

Translate the asset and the bill at the same terminal quote

At the default bill-date quote of 1.50 CAD per FCU, the 10,000 FCU cash balance is worth CAD 15,000. With the unchanged CAD 13,500 cash, the earmarked resources translate to CAD 28,500.

That is CAD 1,500 more than the starting CAD budget. The bill, however, translates to CAD 30,000: 20,000 FCU multiplied by 1.50. It is CAD 3,000 more expensive than at the starting quote. The final funding position is therefore CAD 1,500 short.

The group bars show both translations together. The waterfall starts with the reference funding position, adds the foreign cash’s CAD translation change and subtracts the bill’s larger CAD translation change. Its endpoint is a funding position for this goal, not investment profit or a complete household net-worth measure.

04

Check the shortfall in the bill’s own units

At the bill date, the CAD 13,500 portion can buy 9,000 FCU at the assumed 1.50 quote. Adding the 10,000 FCU already held produces 19,000 FCU. That funds 95% of the 20,000 FCU bill and leaves a 1,000 FCU gap.

Keeping the entire starting budget in CAD would instead buy 18,000 FCU at that quote, funding 90% of the bill. Converting the entire default budget at the starting quote would hold 20,000 FCU and fund the fixed bill exactly under the model’s zero-cost, zero-interest assumptions.

The continuous comparison expresses the remaining FCU gap as a percentage of the FCU bill. Zero means exactly funded; values below zero are shortfalls. This percentage measures funding, not an annual investment return. The quote scenarios have no assigned probabilities.

05

Separate a 100% foreign allocation from a 100% funded goal

Putting all available cash into FCU fixes the number of foreign units held in this model. It does not establish that the starting budget was large enough.

For example, CAD 24,300 converted at 1.35 buys 18,000 FCU. A 100% foreign-currency allocation then funds 90% of the 20,000 FCU bill at every terminal quote. The 2,000 FCU shortfall remains, although its CAD translation changes.

The matrix therefore labels allocation on its rows and the share of the bill funded inside its cells. These percentages describe different things. A full currency allocation can coexist with underfunding, while an initially larger budget can leave a surplus.

06

Keep the matching result specific to the stated goal

The comparison assumes the foreign cash can be used directly for the FCU bill. Reporting that cash in CAD is not an instruction to sell it for CAD and buy the foreign currency back. Actual spreads, transfer charges, payment access and settlement timing would need their own amounts and dates.

The cash and bill are also assumed to keep the same currency and nominal FCU amounts. If the goal changes, is cancelled, increases in price or becomes payable in a different currency, the matching calculation changes. This one-goal result does not describe the household’s other expenses or assets.

For a practical plan, record each bill’s currency, amount and due date beside the accessible cash allocated to it. Then calculate the remaining need in the payment currency and translate the resulting gap into CAD for the broader budget. The charts isolate that arithmetic without selecting an account, forecasting exchange rates or establishing suitability.
